newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech Sept CPI seen quickening but not dangerously.
newsitem.headline: Czech Sept CPI seen quickening but not dangerously.

text.p: Czech monthly consumer inflation, after a brief respite in August, should quicken slightly in September although not to a dangerous level, a Reuters survey of seven economists showed on Monday.

The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) is scheduled to release September CPI data on Tuesday at 0700 GMT, and most economists forecast an increase of about 0.6 percent month-on-month, up from 0.2 percent in August.
Between May and July, the monthly inflation rate accelerated 20 basis points a month to 1.0 percent in July.

If the predicted increase or higher occurs, the government's annual average inflation target for this year, which was recently raised to 8.3 percent from 8.0, remains achievable but difficult to meet, analysts said.
"There weren't any major factors that have me expecting any big movement in the (CPI) rate either way," said Kamil Janacek, chief economist at Komercni Banka.

A 0.6-percent jump in September inflation would put the average annual rate at just under nine percent, Janacek added. Year-on-year inflation in August was 9.6 percent and the 12-month average in the same month was 8.6 percent.

Others said several measures adopted by the central bank to choke inflationary pressures should help September's result. But they said a large increase may force it to consider taking further measures.

"We should now be seeing the full effects of the central bank's measures. And if inflation is higher than expected, it may spook (the Czech National Bank) enough that interest rates could go even slightly higher," said one analyst.
"But it must be careful not to slow economic growth any further," he added.

In determining inflationary pressures, the central bank has been carefully watching monetary growth. July M2 money rose by a year-on-year rate of 17.6 percent, just above what is believed to be its 14-17 percent target range but still its lowest level in several months.

In response to pressures brought about by the rise earlier in the year, the Czech National Bank (CNB) raised its discount rate in June to 10.5 percent from 9.5 and the last-resort Lombard rate to 14 percent from 12.5 to help combat inflation.
In another move to tighten commercial banks' belts, the CNB also raised minimum reserve requirements to 11.5 percent of primary deposits from 8.5 percent as of August 1.
